overview.title: Contents (continued): chapters 8-11
overview.main_topic: Contents entries for the rest of chapter 8 (image classification), chapter 9 (ConvNet architecture patterns), chapter 10 (interpreting what ConvNets learn) and the first two sections of chapter 11 (image segmentation).
overview.central_idea: The computer-vision part of the book moves from training small ConvNets and reusing pretrained ones, to modern architecture patterns, to interpreting what ConvNets learn, and on to segmentation.
overview.importance: It shows the progression of the vision chapters and where key architectural ideas (residual connections, batch normalization, depthwise separable convolutions, Vision Transformers) are introduced.

summary:
This contents page (printed x in the header) continues the vision part of the book.

**Chapter 8 (continued).** 8.2 trains a ConvNet from scratch on a small dataset (printed 241, PDF p.265): why deep learning is relevant for small-data problems, downloading the data, building the model, data preprocessing and **data augmentation**. 8.3 uses a pretrained model (printed 256, PDF p.280): **feature extraction** and **fine-tuning**.

**Chapter 9, ConvNet architecture patterns (printed 268, PDF p.292)** has six flat sections: modularity, hierarchy and reuse; **residual connections**; **batch normalization**; **depthwise separable convolutions**; putting it together in a mini Xception-like model; and, beyond convolution, **Vision Transformers**.

**Chapter 10, Interpreting what ConvNets learn (printed 284, PDF p.308)** covers visualizing intermediate activations, visualizing ConvNet filters via gradient ascent (with separate TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX versions plus the filter visualization loop), visualizing heatmaps of class activation (getting the gradient of the top class in each of the three frameworks, then displaying the heatmap), and visualizing the latent space of a ConvNet.

**Chapter 11, Image segmentation (printed 308, PDF p.332)** begins with computer-vision tasks and the types of image segmentation (11.1), then training a segmentation model from scratch (11.2: downloading a segmentation dataset, building and training the model). Section 11.3 continues on the next page.

Note the multi-backend pattern: where low-level gradient code is required (chapter 10), the book gives one version per framework, echoing chapter 3.

paragraphs.excerpt: The relevance of deep learning for small-data problems 242 Downloading the data
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 8.2 'Training a ConvNet from scratch on a small dataset' lists the relevance of deep learning for small-data problems (242), downloading the data (242), building your model (245), data preprocessing (247) and using data augmentation (252).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The book shows that a ConvNet can be trained on a small image dataset, with augmentation used to fight overfitting.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Data augmentation is a standard tool for small vision datasets and links back to chapter 5's generalization techniques.

terminology.meaning: generating plausible variations of training images (e.g. flips, rotations) to reduce overfitting

connections: p.266: deep learning for small-data problems (printed 242)

paragraphs.excerpt: Feature extraction with a pretrained model 256 ■ Fine-tuning a pretrained model
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 8.3 'Using a pretrained model' lists feature extraction with a pretrained model (256) and fine-tuning a pretrained model (264).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two ways to reuse a network trained on a large dataset: use it as a fixed feature extractor, or partially retrain it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Pretrained-model reuse reappears for segmentation (SAM), detection (RetinaNet), text (Transformers) and LLMs.

terminology.meaning: running inputs through a pretrained network's convolutional base and training a new classifier on top
unfreezing some top layers of a pretrained model and training them jointly with the new head

paragraphs.excerpt: Modularity, hierarchy, and reuse 269 9.2 Residual connections 272 9.3 Batch normalization
paragraphs.what_it_says: This merged element lists all of chapter 9 — modularity, hierarchy and reuse (269), residual connections (272), batch normalization (276), depthwise separable convolutions (278), a mini Xception-like model (280), Vision Transformers (282) — and the start of chapter 10: visualizing intermediate activations (285) and visualizing ConvNet filters (291).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Chapter 9 distills modern architecture best practices into named patterns and combines them in one model; chapter 10 opens with ways to look inside a trained ConvNet.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These patterns (especially residual connections and normalization) are reused well beyond vision, e.g. in Transformers.

terminology.meaning: adding a block's input to its output so information and gradients bypass the block
normalizing intermediate activations using batch statistics
a spatial per-channel convolution followed by a 1x1 pointwise convolution
a Transformer applied to sequences of image patches

paragraphs.excerpt: Gradient ascent in TensorFlow 294 ■ Gradient ascent in PyTorch 295 ■
paragraphs.what_it_says: Under 10.2, the subsections are gradient ascent in TensorFlow (294), in PyTorch (295), in JAX (295), and the filter visualization loop (296).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Filter visualization finds an input that maximally activates a filter by gradient ascent on the input; since this needs raw gradient code, it is given for each backend.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows the gradient machinery of chapters 2-3 used for a new purpose: optimizing inputs instead of weights.

terminology.meaning: repeatedly moving an input in the direction of the gradient to increase a target value

paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 10.3 'Visualizing heatmaps of class activation' lists getting the gradient of the top class in TensorFlow (302), PyTorch (302) and JAX (303), and displaying the class activation heatmap (304).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Class activation heatmaps show which image regions drove a classification decision.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A practical tool for debugging and explaining vision models.

terminology.meaning: a map over the input image of how strongly each region contributed to a predicted class

paragraphs.excerpt: Downloading a segmentation dataset 311 ■ Building and training the segmentation model
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 11.2 'Training a segmentation model from scratch' lists downloading a segmentation dataset (311) and building and training the segmentation model (314).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Segmentation predicts a class for every pixel; the chapter first builds such a model from scratch before using a pretrained one in 11.3.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mirrors chapter 8's structure: from scratch first, then pretrained.

deeper.title: Using printed vs. PDF page numbers
deeper.body: The numbers in this table of contents are the book's printed page numbers. This companion links by PDF page number. For the main body of the book, **PDF page = printed page + 24** (for example, chapter 9 starts on printed page 268, which is PDF p.292; chapter 11 on printed 308, PDF p.332). The offset was checked against the chapter-opener pages; it is a property of this PDF, not something the book states.

misconceptions.claim: The page numbers in the contents are the PDF page numbers.
misconceptions.correction: They are printed page numbers. In this PDF the main body is offset by 24 pages (e.g. printed 16 = PDF p.40).

later.note: 8.2 training a ConvNet from scratch on a small dataset.
Chapter 10 opener: interpreting what ConvNets learn.

takeaways: Chapter 8 contrasts training from scratch (with data augmentation) against reusing pretrained models (feature extraction, fine-tuning).
Chapter 9 names the key ConvNet design patterns and ends with Vision Transformers.
Chapter 10's interpretation methods are shown in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
Chapter 11 starts with segmentation from scratch.

questions.question: Which chapter introduces residual connections and batch normalization?
questions.explanation: Sections 9.2 and 9.3 (printed 272 and 276; PDF p.296 and p.300). The other chapters cover classification, interpretation and segmentation.

questions.question: What are the two ways of using a pretrained model listed in section 8.3?
Why do sections 10.2 and 10.3 have separate TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX subsections when most of the book uses backend-agnostic Keras code?
questions.answer: Because those techniques need direct gradient computations (gradient ascent on inputs, gradient of the top class), which are written with each framework's own gradient API.
questions.explanation: Inference from the subsection titles, consistent with chapter 3 introducing each framework's gradient mechanism.

questions.question: What is the last section of chapter 9 about?
questions.answer: Going beyond convolution: Vision Transformers (printed 282, PDF p.306).

questions.answer: Data augmentation: printed 252 (PDF p.276). Fine-tuning: printed 264 (PDF p.288).
